# Vanishing coarse mass with a full hull: exact limits and a face obstruction

Historical claim of scope (pending review here): proved examples and a geometric reduction. The positive
limiting coarse mass hypothesis in
`candidate 0639bd50a01557c4` cannot
be dropped merely by normalizing the measures to probability. This
remains true when every prelimit body is its actual integer-fiber hull
and the bodies are uniformly normalized. The examples below are not
OC counterexamples.

## 1. A full-dimensional tetrahedral limit with two vanishing fibers

Use coordinates (z,v,x) in R times R^2 and the coarse mixed set
Z times R^2. For 0<epsilon<=1 define two triangles

    Q_0(epsilon)={-1<=v<=1, |x|<=epsilon(v+1)/2},
    Q_1(epsilon)={-1<=x<=1, |v|<=epsilon(x+1)/2},

and put

    C_epsilon=conv(({0} times Q_0) union ({1} times Q_1)).   (1)

The only coarse integer fibers are Q_0,Q_1; each has area 2epsilon.
Both are positive full-dimensional fibers. Thus

    C_epsilon=conv(C_epsilon intersect (Z times R^2)),
    M_epsilon=4epsilon ->0.                               (2)

Nevertheless the Hausdorff limit is the full-dimensional tetrahedron

    C_0={0<=z<=1, |v|<=1-z, |x|<=z}.                      (3)

Its vertices are (0,1,0),(0,-1,0),(1,0,1),(1,0,-1), and its volume
is integral_0^1 4z(1-z) dz=2/3. Each triangle in (1) contains its
limiting segment, so C_0 subset C_epsilon.

This is already an example in a fixed block normalization. The map

    F(z,v,x)=2sqrt(2)(z-1/2,v,x)                          (4)

preserves the continuous subspace. The four facet planes of C_0 have
distance 1/(2sqrt(2)) from (1/2,0,0), so F(C_0) contains the unit ball.
Every C_epsilon is contained in [0,1] times [-1,1]^2, whence

    B_2^3 subset F(C_epsilon) subset 3sqrt(2) B_2^3.

The transformed coarse lattice is 2sqrt(2)Z-sqrt(2), a fixed lattice
coset. Its fiber Jacobian is fixed, so all transformed coarse areas
still tend to zero. In particular this phenomenon is not caused by
failure to replace C by conv(S), or by an ambient hull collapsing.

## 2. The probability limit and an exact jump in maximal depth

Let mu_epsilon be uniform area on the two integer fibers, divided by
4epsilon. For every continuous test function phi on the common compact
box, direct integration gives

    lim integral phi dmu_epsilon
      = integral_(-1)^1 (t+1)/4 phi(0,t,0) dt
        + integral_(-1)^1 (t+1)/4 phi(1,0,t) dt.            (5)

Call this probability measure mu_*. Its two fibers have equal mass,
but their densities along the limiting segments are nonuniform. It is
not the normalized intrinsic H^1 measure of the limiting mixed set.

For every epsilon>0,

    max_(y in C_epsilon intersect (Z times R^2))
                    depth_(mu_epsilon)(y)=2/9.           (6)

Indeed, in a triangle the three caps lambda_i>=1/3, for its barycentric
coordinates, each have relative area 4/9 and cover the triangle.
Extend each such cap from the base 0 fiber by subtracting a sufficiently
large multiple of z from its margin; it then excludes the entire base
1 fiber. Likewise extend the base 1 caps by adding a sufficiently large
multiple of z-1. These six actual ambient caps cover the mixed set and
each has mass 2/9. This proves the upper bound. The ordinary centroid
of either triangle has every containing cap of its own fiber of
relative area at least Gamma_2=4/9, by continuous Grünbaum, giving the
matching lower bound. These are all ambient caps, not a restricted
family of directions.

On the other hand,

    max_(y in C_0 intersect (Z times R^2)) depth_(mu_*)(y)=1/4.
                                                               (7)

On either limiting segment the conditional distribution has cumulative
function (t+1)^2/4 and median sqrt(2)-1. At this median every ambient
halfspace contains at least half of its own segment's probability,
including the case where the entire segment lies in the boundary.
Thus its total depth is at least 1/4. Conversely, at any point on
either segment a one-sided interval of conditional probability at most
1/2 can be isolated from the other fiber by a finite integer tilt.
This proves the upper bound.

The measures in (5) converge weakly, but their maximum depths do not
converge to the limit's maximum depth. There is already a fixed closed
halfspace witnessing failure of uniform cap convergence:

    H={x-2z>=0},
    mu_epsilon(H)=1/4,   mu_*(H)=1/2.                    (8)

At base 0 it cuts each thin triangle in half but contains the entire
limiting segment; at base 1 it excludes the source completely. The
boundary mass in (8) cannot be discarded.

## 3. The same hull limit supports many different probability laws

More generally let f,g be fixed continuous nonnegative concave
functions on [-1,1], neither identically zero. Replace the two fibers
by

    {-1<=v<=1, |x|<=epsilon f(v)},
    {-1<=x<=1, |v|<=epsilon g(x)}.

They are convex, have areas 2epsilon integral f and
2epsilon integral g, and still contain the same two limiting segments.
Their hulls therefore have exactly the same limit (3). Their normalized
weak limit is

    (integral f+integral g)^(-1)
       [f(t)dt on (0,t,0) + g(t)dt on (1,0,t)].            (9)

This follows by the change of variables x=epsilon f(v)s, -1<=s<=1,
and its counterpart on the other fiber, followed by bounded
convergence. Constant profiles with different positive values give
arbitrary positive relative masses on the same two uniform segments.
Nonconstant profiles give nonuniform densities. The full geometric
limit of the hull does not determine the probability limit.

## 4. An actual one-fine/one-finite lattice sequence

The preceding example also occurs with n=2,d=1 and a genuinely fine
integer direction. Let ell be a positive integer, put

    epsilon=1/ell,   h=1/ell^2,

and sample (1) on the base lattice Z times hZ in coordinates (z,v).
Equivalently, in the original standard lattice coordinates (z,k,x),
take the inverse image under (z,k,x)->(z,hk,x). All vertices of (1)
are sampled: their v coordinates are -1,0,1,-epsilon,epsilon, all in
hZ. Hence each body is still EXACTLY the convex hull of its actual
mixed set. This is an explicit diagonal lattice splitting, with one
finite and one fine direction; no general lattice-reduction theorem
is asserted.

Multiply the sampled length measure by h, which does not change its
normalized depth. Its exact masses at the two coarse bases are

    M_(ell,0)=2/ell+1/ell^3,
    M_(ell,1)=2/ell,
    M_ell=4/ell+1/ell^3.                                 (10)

For base 0 the lengths are epsilon(kh+1), -ell^2<=k<=ell^2.
For base 1 they are 2-2|k|/ell, -ell<=k<=ell. Summation gives (10),
including the zero-length endpoint fibers exactly.

These normalized sampled measures have the same weak limit (5).
One direct verification couples each occupied base cell with its
sampled fiber: moving v by at most h/2 changes a continuous test by
its modulus of continuity. The absolute difference between the
cell union and its coarse convex fiber is O(h), by the same convex
dilation/erosion estimate used in the sampling theorem. Division by
M_epsilon=4/ell makes the error O(1/ell), tending to zero. Combine
this with (5).

Their maximal normalized depths satisfy

    lim_ell max depth_(sampled measure)=2/9,              (11)

not the value 1/4 of the weak probability limit. Here are full cap and
center checks. On each of the two coarse fibers the sampling theorem
with r=s=1,R=1,delta=h/2 bounds the absolute cap error by 2h+h^2.
Their sum is E_ell=4h+2h^2. Since the exact total discrepancy in (10)
is 1/ell^3 and M_ell>=4/ell, normalized cap discrepancy is at most

    E_ell/M_ell+(1/ell^3)/M_ell
      <=1/ell+1/(4ell^2)+1/(2ell^3) <=2/ell.              (12)

Every sampled point is a feasible coarse point, so (6) and (12) give
the upper limit in (11). For the lower limit start at the centroid
(0,1/3,0) of the first coarse triangle and round only v to its nearest
h-grid point. For ell>=2 the resulting point remains in that triangle.
Every section of either coarse triangle has length at most 2sqrt(2).
Thus the normalized coarse depth is Lipschitz in (v,x) with constant
at most 4sqrt(2)/(4/ell)=sqrt(2)ell. The rounding loss is at most
sqrt(2)/(2ell). Equation (12) now proves the lower limit. All pure
base normals and all closed boundary caps are included in that estimate.

Applying the fixed map (4) gives unit inner ball and a uniform outer
ball, while the base lattice has exactly the two spacings
2sqrt(2) and 2sqrt(2)/ell^2. The example therefore survives a genuine
block normalization of conv(S).

## 5. A necessary geometric consequence: the coarse projection is hollow

Here is what the full hull DOES force. Let P be a finite lattice-convex
set spanning R^k and let compact nonempty convex fibers Q_j in R^m be
convex-compatible at its integer bases. Suppose their lifted hull D
is full dimensional in R^(k+m), but

    vol_m(Q_j)=0 for every j in P.                        (13)

Then

    int(conv(P)) intersect Z^k is empty.                  (14)

Proof: any fiber of a full-dimensional convex body over an interior
point of its projection is full dimensional. For completeness, choose
an interior ball at a point above p_0. For a prescribed interior base p,
choose q in the projection slightly beyond p on the ray from p_0, so
p=(1-t)p_0+tq with t<1; if p=p_0 use the original ball. Combining the
interior ball with any point over q gives a positive-radius continuous
ball in the fiber over p. Compatibility makes D_j=Q_j at all j in P,
and lattice-convexity says P=conv(P) intersect Z^k. An interior integer
base would therefore contradict (13).

For k=0 this rules out (13) altogether. For k=1, full dimension and
lattice-convexity force

    P={a,a+1} for an integer a.                           (15)

Thus the zero-coarse-mass case with ONE remaining coarse integer
coordinate has an exact two-slice reduction, rather than an arbitrary
collection of disappearing fibers. For a prelimit family whose coarse
support is this SAME fixed set P, the prelimit sources likewise have
only those two coarse slices. If there are no additional fine integer
coordinates and the prelimit fibers have positive full d-volume, they
are two ordinary convex bodies. The heavier has at least half the
source mass; its continuous centroid immediately gives depth at least
Gamma_d/2. If there are r additional integer coordinates and the two
prelimit coarse slices are full-dimensional bodies in R^(r+d), the
analogous conclusion follows conditionally from OC(r,d) on the heavier
slice, paying exactly one factor 1/2. A lower-dimensional endpoint
slice would instead require the separate relative/intrinsic reduction;
no such reduction or OC(r,d) assertion is supplied by this conditional
step. The abstract limiting-hull lemma
alone does not assert eventual equality of an otherwise varying
prelimit support with P.

This consequence requires both the full-dimensional limiting HULL
and actual compatibility of its integer fibers. Full ambient limits
unrelated to the fiber hull do not suffice.

## 6. Rank two: no universal half-mass supporting face

The extension of (15) to a single lower-rank face carrying half the
mass is false. Let the coarse projection be the lattice triangle

    Q=conv((0,0),(2,0),(0,2)),

with barycentric coordinates lambda_0,lambda_1,lambda_2. In continuous
dimension 3 define

    D_epsilon={z in Q: |x_i|<=epsilon+(1-epsilon)lambda_i(z),
                         i=0,1,2},   0<epsilon<1.         (16)

All displayed constraints are affine inequalities, so this is convex.
It equals the hull of its three vertex fibers: at a real base z the
Minkowski combination of those boxes is precisely the displayed box,
because its half-widths are affine. Those vertices have integer bases,
so D_epsilon=conv(D_epsilon intersect (Z^2 times R^3)).

The projection Q has exactly six integer points, its three vertices
and three edge midpoints. Their respective fiber volumes are

    w_vertex=8epsilon^2,
    w_midpoint=2epsilon(1+epsilon)^2.                     (17)

All tend to zero. Nonetheless D_0 has full ambient dimension five:
at an interior base all three lambda_i are positive, and hence the
fiber contains a three-dimensional box; the strict displayed
inequalities also persist for a neighborhood of that base. A fixed
block normalization of D_0 therefore normalizes the entire bounded
family uniformly, exactly as in Section 1.

After total-mass normalization, (17) puts limiting probability 1/3
on each edge-midpoint fiber, which is a two-dimensional square, and
zero on the three vertex fibers. The total mass and the mass above
any projection edge are

    M=24epsilon^2+6epsilon(1+epsilon)^2,
    M_edge=16epsilon^2+2epsilon(1+epsilon)^2.

They satisfy the exact strict inequality

    M-2 M_edge=2epsilon(1-epsilon)^2>0.                   (18)

Every proper supporting face of the projection is either an edge or
a vertex. None carries half of the prelimit mass, and none carries
more than 1/3 of the limiting probability. In particular no argument
using only the fact that the projection is hollow may select one
supporting face and charge a single factor 1/2 as in (15).

The three projection edges do give an exhaustive lower-rank cover in
this example; they do not by themselves yield the sharp global
power-of-two induction budget. Equation (18) rules out the naive
heavy-face strengthening, not every possible mass-weighted facet
decomposition. No general sharp face-decomposition theorem is claimed.

## 7. What remains after this obstruction

There are three different data levels: the full ambient hull, the
normalized probability limit, and cap masses along moving normals.
Equations (3), (5), and (6)--(8) show that the first two do not retain
the third when coarse volume vanishes. The hollow-projection lemma
is a genuine geometric restriction, and in coarse rank one it yields
the exact two-slice reduction. Higher-rank face budgets and preservation
of the vanishing transverse geometry remain additional requirements.
Neither probability renormalization nor an arbitrary canonical lift
of the limiting marginal is asserted to preserve those cap constraints.
